pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 8–9 years

- **Topic:** Reading Food Web Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans'):** pupils construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey — reading a web is the natural extension, tracing many overlapping chains through one diagram.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 5-LS2-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-LS2-1] — a food web IS that model, and reading it fluently is the entry skill.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL topic — the concept (feeding relationships) is already known; the new learning is decoding the diagram convention. The single load-bearing rule is arrow direction: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, i.e. in the direction energy/matter flows. Children read a web by (a) naming producers vs consumers, (b) tracing a single chain through the tangle, (c) finding an organism that appears in several chains, and (d) predicting what happens downstream when one organism is removed. Keep webs to 6–8 organisms at this age so the arrows stay legible.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational). The child works with a concrete, pictured web of familiar organisms and answers 'who eats whom' and 'what if' by tracing arrows — no quantities, no energy maths yet. Success = can trace any chain and correctly reason one step of removal-cascade.
bestPractices: Front-load the arrow-direction convention explicitly and check it before any web reading: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, the way energy flows. Most reading errors trace back to this one rule.
Start from a single chain the child can already read, then overlay a second and third that share an organism — build the web up from chains rather than presenting the full tangle cold.
Teach three read-moves in order: name the roles (producer/consumer), trace one chain end-to-end, then find a shared organism that sits in several chains.
Use 'what if we remove this?' prediction as the culminating task — it turns passive reading into causal reasoning and reveals whether the child sees the web as interconnected.
Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; complexity should come from interconnection, not from unfamiliar species.
keyRepresentations: Pictured food web (nodes = organism images, directed arrows = energy flow) — the canonical diagram to decode
Single highlighted chain traced through the web (grass → rabbit → fox) to show a web is many overlapping chains
Role colour-coding: producers one colour, consumers another, to make structure pop
Removal 'ripple': greying one node and dimming every arrow and organism downstream of it
commonMisconceptions: Drawing/reading the arrow backwards — pointing from the eater to the food (thinking the arrow means 'eats') rather than in the direction energy flows.
Believing a web is just one long chain, so removing an organism only affects the next one along, not every path it feeds.
Thinking arrows show 'who is bigger/stronger' rather than what eats what.
Assuming an organism can only be in one chain, missing that many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains.

learn.summary: Teaching 8–9-year-olds to read and interpret food web diagrams. The concept of feeding relationships is already known; the new learning is decoding the diagram convention — above all the arrow-direction rule: the arrow points FROM the food TO the eater, in the direction energy/matter flows. Learners name producers vs consumers, trace a single chain through the tangle, find organisms shared by several chains, and predict knock-on effects of removing a species. Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; complexity should come from interconnection, not unfamiliar species.

activities.title: Lock in the arrow-direction rule first
feedback: If a learner draws bird → caterpillar or says the arrow means 'eats', re-label the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to' and have them re-check that every arrowhead points toward the feeder.

If a learner describes 'who is connected to who' but cannot state a direction, they are ignoring arrowheads: reteach the directed-diagram convention (like a one-way street sign) — the arrowhead carries the meaning, not just the line.
When a learner can both read a given arrow correctly AND draw an unaided one pointing the right way, they have produced the convention, not just recognised it.
activities.rationale: This is a representational topic whose single load-bearing rule is arrow direction; most reading errors trace to it, so front-load and check it explicitly before any web reading. Drawing one unaided — and testing it by reversing a chain — catches a child who recognises but cannot produce the convention.
sourceClaims: Food-web arrow convention: the arrow points from the organism being eaten toward the organism that eats it, showing the direction of energy/matter flow; reversing it is the classic pupil misconception.
learnerActions: Look at a single arrow between two pictured organisms, e.g. grass → rabbit, and say exactly what it means: the arrow points to the eater, so energy/matter flows FROM grass TO rabbit.
Given 'a caterpillar and a bird that eats it', draw the arrow yourself, pointing the right way (caterpillar → bird).
Check every arrowhead in a small web points toward the feeder, re-reading each as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'.

Redraw a three-species chain with all its arrows reversed and decide whether it still makes sense — it does not, because energy would then appear to flow from the eater back to its food, the opposite of how feeding works.
activities.intendedInsight: The arrowhead carries the meaning: it shows the direction energy/matter travels, from food to feeder — not 'this eats that'.

activities.title: Build the web up from chains and name the roles
feedback: If a learner can trace one chain but gets lost where an animal feeds two predators, scaffold by highlighting that one animal and following every arrow leaving it; the concept is present, only the diagram-tracing needs practice — do not reteach the arrow meaning.

In a web that shows every organism's food, a producer (a plant) has food arrows only leaving it and none arriving. Use this as a quick role-check, but confirm that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn would look the same.
activities.rationale: Building from a known single chain to overlapping chains makes the mesh legible and prevents the misconception that a web is just one long chain. Role-naming is the entry read-move before tracing and prediction.
sourceClaims: DfE Y4 'Animals, including humans' requires pupils to construct and interpret a variety of food chains, identifying producers, predators and prey.
learnerActions: Start from one chain you can already read (grass → rabbit → fox); then overlay a second and third chain that share an organism, so the web grows from chains rather than appearing as a full tangle.

Name each organism's role: producers (plants, which make their own food using sunlight) and consumers; then split the consumers into primary consumers (eat producers) and secondary consumers (eat other consumers). If decomposers (e.g. fungi, worms, bacteria) are shown, name them as feeders on dead material and waste. Notice that a producer has no food arrows arriving at it, but check that it is a plant, because an animal whose food is not drawn in the web would also have only arrows leaving it.
Trace one chain end-to-end with a finger, saying the running label aloud (grass → rabbit → fox).
activities.intendedInsight: A food web is many overlapping chains, and each organism plays a role (producer, primary consumer, secondary consumer, or decomposer if shown) that you can read from the diagram.

activities.title: Find shared organisms at crossing points
feedback: If a learner assumes each organism belongs to only one chain, pick an animal that feeds two predators and trace both chains through it together.
Praise finding a node where multiple chains meet: this is the structural feature that makes a web more than a single chain.
activities.rationale: Addresses the misconception that an organism can only be in one chain; locating shared nodes is the read-move that reveals interconnection and prepares for removal-cascade reasoning.
learnerActions: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in the web.
Highlight one organism and follow every arrow that touches it to see how many chains cross there.
activities.intendedInsight: Many organisms sit at the crossing point of several chains — a web is a mesh, not a set of separate lines.

activities.title: Predict the ripple when a species is removed
feedback: If a learner says only the next organism along is affected, have them follow each arrow leaving the removed organism (these point to the animals that ate it) to reveal multiple dependents — e.g. removing rabbits can affect both the fox and the owl that fed on them.
If prediction is correct, ask them to justify it by naming the specific paths that break.
activities.rationale: 'What if we remove this?' turns passive reading into causal reasoning and reveals whether the child sees the web as interconnected — the point where reading a web becomes reasoning with a web.
learnerActions: Pick an organism (e.g. rabbits) and, following the arrows, predict whose food disappears if it is removed.
Trace along every path the removed organism fed — not just the next one along — and name each organism affected downstream.
Explain to a partner or an 'ecologist' character why removing one node can affect more than one other animal.
activities.intendedInsight: Removing one node ripples along EVERY path it fed: because a web is interconnected, one removal can affect several organisms, not just the next one in a single chain.

activities.title: Optional interactive web-reader and companion reference
feedback: Use a quick arrow-direction gate before free exploration (tap the arrow showing energy flowing from grass to rabbit) so the convention is secured first.
Include an arrow-direction distractor (an arrow drawn eater→food) as the classic misconception check when assessing reading.
activities.rationale: These interaction and feedback examples (tap-to-highlight, drag-to-trace with a running label, remove-button ripple, lift-the-flap annotations) are offered as untested options to make the learning mechanism concrete; the same moves can be done on paper by tracing chains and greying out a removed organism. The static annotated web teaches the convention crisply but does not by itself let a learner do the removal-cascade prediction, so pair it with an activity where learners predict ripples themselves.
learnerActions: On an interactive pictured web of 6–8 familiar organisms (grass, rabbit, mouse, fox, owl, beetle, hawk), tap an organism so every arrow it touches lights up, revealing the mesh of relationships.
Drag a fingertip from grass through rabbit to fox to trace a single chain, with a running 'grass → rabbit → fox' label naming it.

Press a 'remove' button on an organism and watch the arrows leaving it dim and the organisms that fed on it (e.g. fox AND owl after removing the rabbit) light up as losing one food source. They do not automatically disappear if the web shows they have other food (e.g. a fox that also eats mice).

As a pre-teach reference, use a static annotated web with lift-the-flaps: tap each arrow to reveal 'the arrow points to the eater — energy flows this way', tap each node to reveal its producer/predator/prey role.
activities.intendedInsight: Interactive highlighting, tracing, and a visible removal-ripple can make the mesh structure and the knock-on effects of removal concrete and felt.

constraints: This is Tier A (concrete/observational): work with a concrete, pictured web of familiar organisms; no quantities and no energy maths yet. Success = can trace any chain and correctly reason one step of a removal-cascade.
Keep webs to 6–8 familiar local organisms so arrows stay legible; let complexity come from interconnection, not unfamiliar species.
Front-load and check the arrow-direction convention before any web reading, since most reading errors trace to it.

A recognition-only or multiple-choice response checks reading but does not require the learner to produce the convention; include at least one task where the learner draws an arrow unaided to confirm production, not just recognition.
A static annotated web is a strong reference/pre-teach for the convention but does not by itself elicit independent removal-cascade prediction; pair it with a prediction task.
A dialogue/'explain your thinking' layer can probe reasoning but is best as a follow-up to visual tracing, since the core skill is visual-spatial diagram reading.

To identify which organisms lose a food source when one is removed, follow the arrows LEAVING the removed organism (they point to the animals that ate it); arrows arriving at it come from its own food, which may then be eaten less.
The removal-ripple shows which organisms lose a food source; at this age treat it as 'whose food disappears / is affected' rather than precise population modelling.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source's arrow-direction claim is marked verified:false in the row; treat the convention statement as standard science-education guidance pending confirmation. The two standards citations (DfE Y4, NGSS 5-LS2-1) are marked verified:true.

NGSS 5-LS2-1 ('food web is that model') and DfE Y4 are topic/standards-level citations; they are not attached to individual activities whose specific teaching principle (arrow front-loading, removal-cascade prediction, interactive-media affordances) they do not directly support. sourceClaims were trimmed to [] on those activities rather than invent support.

The original row asserted a 3D rendering 'adds nothing' / is 'actively worse' and that dialogue 'cannot show the web being traced'. These are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy claims; retained only as scoped notes that a flat graph is easier to trace without depth/occlusion and that dialogue is best as a follow-up probe. No universal necessity is claimed.

The original framed the interactive 2D reader as uniquely 'ideal' and the quiz as testing 'rather than building' intuition. These catalog rankings have been reframed as optional media and complementary roles; the underlying learner actions are preservable on paper, and efficacy of the interactive version is untested.

probeDeeper: Trace two different food chains that both pass through the same animal in this web.
If I rub out the rabbits, follow the arrows — whose food disappears?
Which organism has arrows only leaving it and none arriving? What does that tell you it is?
Redraw this three-species chain with all the arrows reversed — would it still make sense? Why not?
assess.correctAnswer: The arrow means 'is eaten by' — energy travels in the direction of the arrowhead, from the food to the feeder. The drawn arrow therefore goes FROM the caterpillar TO the bird (caterpillar → bird).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The arrow points to what the animal eats' — reads it as 'eats' and reverses direction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-label the arrow as 'is eaten by / energy goes to'; check every arrowhead points toward the feeder.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the arrow means 'this eats that' and draws bird → caterpillar.

errorPatterns.pattern: Ignores arrowheads — reads the web as unordered links and cannot state a direction.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach the directed-diagram convention (as with circuit diagrams): the arrowhead carries the meaning, not just the line.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes 'who is connected to who' but cannot say which way energy goes.

errorPatterns.pattern: Traces along lines but cannot find species shared by two chains — misreads branching points.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold: highlight one animal and follow every arrow leaving it; the concept is present, the diagram-tracing needs practice. Do not reteach the arrow meaning.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Follows one chain fine but gets lost where an animal feeds two predators.

responseLevels.gap: Reads arrows as 'eats' or ignores direction entirely; cannot draw a correctly-pointed arrow.
responseLevels.full: Reads arrow direction as energy flow, produces a correctly-directed arrow on demand, and traces multiple chains through the web, identifying shared species and predicting removal effects from the diagram.
responseLevels.partial: Interprets a single arrow correctly and identifies a producer/consumer, but stumbles tracing two chains through a shared species.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show a food web diagram. First: 'Point to one arrow and tell me exactly what it means — which way does the food and energy travel along it?' Then: 'Now I name two animals — a caterpillar and a bird that eats it. Draw the arrow between them yourself, pointing the right way.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The interpret step catches a child who reads the arrow as 'eats' (arrowhead aimed at the food). The translate step — drawing one unaided — catches whether they can PRODUCE the convention, not just recognise it; a child right for the wrong reason draws bird → caterpillar.
